title: Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance - CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance - Intergovernmental Treaties and Trade Agreements
subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: In the United States, how do international trade agreements, such as the WTO Government Procurement Agreement (GPA), primarily affect sub-central (state and local) government procurements?
options: They strictly dictate all local purchasing rules regardless of dollar value.
They prohibit local agencies from buying from foreign vendors.
State and local governments are only bound if their state has voluntarily committed to the agreement and the procurement exceeds a specific dollar threshold.
They require local entities to use federal funds for all international purchases.
questions.explain: International treaties like the WTO GPA apply to US states only if the specific state explicitly opted-in (committed) to the agreement. Furthermore, the rules only trigger when a specific procurement surpasses high international dollar thresholds.

questions.q: A fundamental principle of international trade agreements (like USMCA or WTO GPA) regarding public procurement is 'National Treatment'. What does this require?
options: Agencies must treat domestic suppliers better than foreign suppliers.
Agencies must treat suppliers from signatory countries no less favorably than they treat their own domestic suppliers.
Procurements must be advertised in the national newspaper of all participating countries.
Only national governments, not local ones, can enter into contracts.
questions.explain: 'National Treatment' is the principle that a government must treat goods, services, and suppliers of other party nations the same as (no less favorably than) its own domestic goods, services, and suppliers.

questions.q: If a procurement is subject to the USMCA (United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement) trade rules, an agency is generally PROHIBITED from:
options: Using clear, technical specifications.
Applying mandatory local geographical preference margins that heavily favor a hometown business over a Canadian bidder.
Evaluating proposals based on best value.
Requiring the vendor to be financially stable.
questions.explain: Trade agreements enforce non-discrimination. When they apply, they typically ban offsets and mandatory local preference laws that automatically disadvantage foreign bidders from signatory nations in favor of domestic/local bidders.

questions.q: If a procurement falls under the purview of a major international trade agreement (like the WTO GPA), which evaluation practice is commonly restricted?
options: Considering the life-cycle costs of an asset.
Demanding offsets (e.g., requiring the foreign vendor to invest back into the local economy).
Evaluating the technical expertise of the foreign firm.
Requiring environmental sustainability certifications.
questions.explain: International trade agreements generally prohibit 'offsets', which are conditions placed on foreign firms requiring them to use local content, license local technology, or invest back into the local economy as a condition of winning a contract.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: When assessing whether an international trade agreement applies to a local procurement, the agency must calculate the 'Estimated Value of the Procurement.' This value must include:
options: Only the first year of the contract.
The base term, plus all possible options, renewals, and potential premiums or fees.
The amount minus local taxes.
Only the labor costs, not the materials.
questions.explain: Trade agreements stipulate that when calculating the value of a procurement to see if it meets the treaty threshold, the agency must estimate the maximum total value over the entire life of the contract, inclusive of all options, renewals, and premiums.
